lead: An air cycle machine cools bleed air by expanding it, so it needs pressurised bleed air and ram air to dump heat. Parked on a hot stand there is no ram air and the bleed is already hot, so many aircraft carry a vapour cycle machine instead. It cools by boiling a refrigerant in an evaporator and condensing it in a condenser, like a domestic refrigerator. This chapter also covers cabin heating: electric elements, hot bleed air through a mixing valve, or a shroud around the exhaust muffler.
prereq: You need the air cycle machine and the bleed air supply first: see Chapter 2.6 and Chapter 2.2.

sections.h3: Why a vapour cycle machine exists

blocks.text: An air cycle machine is an open system. It takes hot bleed air, cools it in a heat exchanger, then expands it through a turbine. Its cooling power depends on two things it cannot control: bleed air pressure and the temperature of the ram air available to the heat exchanger.

Parked on the ground on a 42 °C afternoon in Chennai, both are against you. There is no ram air flow and the bleed is hot, so an air cycle machine on ground cart duty gives poor cooling for a lot of bleed air.

A vapour cycle machine closes the loop. A fixed charge of refrigerant, R-134a for example, is sealed inside pipes and carried round and round; it is not thrown away after each pass. R-134a boils at about −26 °C at sea-level pressure, so it easily becomes colder than the cabin it cools. The machine needs only electrical or shaft power for its compressor, plus a small fan or ram air to cool the condenser.

You meet vapour cycle machines as ground cooling carts, in cargo and galley cooling on some transport aircraft, and in flight deck cooling on a few types. The same four components sit in your kitchen refrigerator and in a split air conditioner.

sections.h3: The four steps of the vapour compression cycle

blocks.text: Follow one kilogram of refrigerant round the loop. It changes from vapour to liquid and back, and that change is where the heat is carried.

items: Compression. The compressor takes low-pressure, low-temperature vapour and squeezes it. Pressure and temperature rise above the outside air temperature, and shaft work is added.

Condensation. The hot high-pressure vapour enters the condenser, a finned heat exchanger. Outside air (ram air in flight, a fan on the ground) takes heat out, and the vapour condenses into a high-pressure liquid.

Expansion. The liquid passes through the expansion valve, a small orifice. Pressure drops sharply and temperature falls with it, giving a cold, low-pressure liquid-vapour mixture. No work is taken out; the process is a throttling.
Evaporation. The cold mixture enters the evaporator in the cabin air duct. Cabin air blows over the fins and gives up heat; the refrigerant boils back to vapour and returns to the compressor.

blocks.where: COP is the coefficient of performance, a pure number; Q<sub>evap</sub> is the heat absorbed from the cabin air in the evaporator, in kW; W<sub>comp</sub> is the shaft work put into the compressor, in kW.
Q<sub>cond</sub> is the heat rejected at the condenser, in kW. The condenser throws away both the cabin heat and the compressor work, so it is always larger than the evaporator.

blocks.text: A well-designed machine reaches a COP of 3 to 5. An air cycle machine at the same low altitude sits near 1 or below, because it compresses air that is then dumped overboard.

items: Works on the ground: no bleed air and no ram air needed, just a small electric condenser fan. This is why ground carts use it.
Higher COP at low altitude: less shaft or electrical power per kW of cabin cooling than an air cycle machine.
The condenser needs good airflow. Dust, leaves and insects raise the condensing temperature and the COP falls fast.
Weight and complexity: a sealed compressor, receiver, pipework and refrigerant charge add mass.
Refrigerant handling: the charge must be recovered and recharged by trained staff; venting to atmosphere is illegal in most countries.
Leakage: joints and shaft seals leak slowly. A low charge shows as poor cooling, a cycling compressor and frost on the wrong pipe.

blocks.text: A cabin at cruise is usually too cold, not too hot. The structure soaks to the outside air temperature, the outside air is below −40 °C at altitude, and the air cycle machine delivers cold air. Without heat the flight deck becomes uncomfortable and windscreens mist and ice over.

Bleed-air trim is the method on large aircraft. Hot bleed air passes through a trim air valve and mixes with the cold air leaving the air cycle machine. A zone controller moves the valve to hold the selected cabin temperature. See Chapter 2.2 for where that bleed comes from.

Electric heaters are resistive elements wound into the air duct, switched by a relay or solid-state controller. They suit small aircraft and helicopters with no bleed air, and also supply foot heat and windshield heat. Windshield heating is covered in Chapter 2.11.

Exhaust muff heat is used on small piston-engine aircraft. A shroud around the muffler collects hot air, and a valve lets the pilot send it to the cabin or dump it overboard. The danger is carbon monoxide: a cracked muffler pushes exhaust gas into the cabin. A CO detector is the standard guard, and the heater valve is normally closed during take-off and climb.

figure.caption: Refrigerant travels round the closed loop; the condenser rejects heat to the outside air while the evaporator takes heat from the cabin. Both heat flows pass through the compressor work.

spec.title: Vapour cycle loop
spec.aria: Refrigerant is compressed, gives up heat in the condenser, is throttled by the expansion valve, absorbs heat in the evaporator and returns to the compressor.

examples.question: A vapour cycle cabin cooling pack absorbs 12 kW from the cabin air. The compressor shaft takes 3 kW. (a) Find the coefficient of performance. (b) Find the heat rejected at the condenser. (c) The same compressor is used in a pack that must reach COP = 3.5. What evaporator load can it now carry?
steps: Write the data: Q<sub>evap</sub> = 12 kW, W<sub>comp</sub> = 3 kW.
Part (a): COP = Q<sub>evap</sub> ÷ W<sub>comp</sub> = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0. The COP has no unit.
Part (b): apply the first law to the whole loop. Q<sub>cond</sub> = Q<sub>evap</sub> + W<sub>comp</sub> = 12 + 3 = 15 kW.
The condenser must dump 15 kW, which is why it needs a large face area and a strong fan or ram air flow.
Part (c): rearrange the COP definition, Q<sub>evap</sub> = COP × W<sub>comp</sub> = 3.5 × 3 = 10.5 kW.
The pack cools less because the same 3 kW of shaft work now moves only 10.5 kW instead of 12 kW out of the cabin.
examples.answer: (a) COP = 4.0; (b) condenser heat rejected = 15 kW; (c) evaporator load at COP 3.5 = 10.5 kW.
examples.check:
Q_evap = 12.0  # kW
W_comp = 3.0    # kW
COP = Q_evap / W_comp
Q_cond = Q_evap + W_comp
Q_evap_new = 3.5 * W_comp
print(COP)
print(Q_cond)
print(Q_evap_new)

traps: Swapping condenser and evaporator. The condenser is the hot one that rejects heat outside; the evaporator is the cold one inside the cabin duct.
Thinking COP above 1 breaks the first law. It does not: the extra heat at the condenser is the compressor work, and Q<sub>cond</sub> = Q<sub>evap</sub> + W<sub>comp</sub> always holds.
Using condenser heat in the COP. COP is Q<sub>evap</sub> ÷ W<sub>comp</sub>, never Q<sub>cond</sub> ÷ W<sub>comp</sub>.
Forgetting that the expansion valve does no work. It only drops pressure and temperature; the compressor is the only work input.
Treating the vapour cycle as an open system like the air cycle machine. It is closed: the same refrigerant charge circulates again and again.

quiz.q: Name the four components of a vapour cycle machine in the order the refrigerant passes through them.
quiz.a: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator, then back to the compressor.

quiz.q: Why does a vapour cycle machine cool better than an air cycle machine when the aircraft is parked on a hot day?
quiz.a: It is a closed loop and needs no bleed air. The condenser only needs a small fan, so the machine is independent of ram air and bleed pressure. Its COP at low altitude is also higher, so the same power removes more heat.

quiz.q: A pack absorbs 18 kW in the evaporator and the compressor shaft takes 4.5 kW. Find the COP and the condenser heat rejection.
quiz.a: COP = 18 ÷ 4.5 = 4.0. Q<sub>cond</sub> = 18 + 4.5 = 22.5 kW rejected to the outside air.

quiz.q: A vapour cycle pack shows COP = 4. A student claims this means the pack delivers four times the energy it consumes. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: The pack does not create energy. It uses 3 kW of shaft work, for example, to move 12 kW of heat from the cabin to the outside air. The work is not the source of the heat; it is the cost of pumping it uphill in temperature. The first law still balances at the condenser: 12 kW in from the cabin plus 3 kW of work equals 15 kW out.

quiz.q: Why does the condenser need a clean, unobstructed airflow?
quiz.a: The condenser can only condense the refrigerant if it dumps heat to the outside air. Blocked or dusty fins raise the condensing temperature and pressure, the compressor works harder, and the COP falls; cooling drops and the compressor may cycle on its high-pressure cut-out.

quiz.q: State two sources of cabin heat used on small aircraft.
quiz.a: A shroud around the engine exhaust muffler feeding hot air to the cabin, and electric resistive heaters in the air duct.

quiz.q: Why is a carbon monoxide detector fitted when cabin heat comes from an exhaust muff shroud?
quiz.a: Cabin air passes over a shroud around the muffler. A crack lets exhaust gas, which contains carbon monoxide, enter the cabin air supply. CO is odourless and binds to haemoglobin, so a detector is the only reliable warning. The heater valve is also closed during take-off and climb when the risk is highest.

beyond: Not for the exam. R-134a is being replaced in new designs because of its high global warming potential; R-1234yf and carbon dioxide (R-744) are the leading candidates, and CO2 systems run at very high pressure. More-electric aircraft push toward electrically driven vapour cycle packs so no bleed air is needed. High-power radar and electronics are cooled by the same principle, sometimes as a two-phase loop.
